title: Chahi Taret: Seven Silent Years
subtitle: When the Valley Emptied and Memory Fought On
region: Kangla, Manipur valley, Cachar and Ava
moral: A people survive when memory refuses to surrender.

sources.citation: Parratt, The Court Chronicle of the Kings of Manipur, Vol. 2 (2009)
sources.note: Meitei court record for the Burmese occupation and liberation period.
Detailed Manipur-centered account of the Seven Years Devastation.

sources.citation: Thant Myint-U, The Making of Modern Burma (Cambridge University Press, 2001)
sources.note: Burmese-side context for deportees and Cassay Horse formations.

panels.shot: wide aerial view over a mist-veiled, abandoned Kangla fort and deserted paddy fields, with a lone Meitei rider in the foreground

dialogue.text: In 1819, the Meitei valley fell silent. This is Chahi Taret Khuntakpa—the Seven Years Devastation—when a kingdom emptied but a people refused to die in memory.

panels.shot: slow push-in from above onto Kangla fort bustling in earlier times, contrasting with the later silence

dialogue.text: Only years before, Kangla was alive. Kings of Manipur held court, rituals burned bright, and the valley’s rice-fields fed a proud kingdom.

panels.shot: medium interior shot in the dim palace hall with tense, shadowed figures

dialogue.text: But behind the drums of ritual came whispers of succession. Princes quarrelled over Kangla’s throne, each seeking allies beyond the misty hills.

panels.shot: dramatic side shot of a Meitei envoy before a distant Burmese palace, with Ava’s skyline in the haze

dialogue.text: More than once, Meitei princes rode to Ava and asked the Burmese kings for troops. Politics opened the door that later swallowed the valley.

panels.shot: wide low-angle of a Burmese host on the march over the eastern ridges towards Manipur

dialogue.text: In 1819, under Bodawpaya’s successors, the Burmese army marched west again. This time, the march did not end with a quick kingmaking.

panels.shot: chaotic wide shot of the Manipur plain as the Burmese army descends, smoke rising in the distance

dialogue.text: Meitei chronicles and later scholars describe the invasion as a devastation. The Burmese forces overran the valley, broke resistance, and made occupation their aim.

panels.shot: somber medium shot of villagers bound together and marched, with Ava’s direction indicated by distant hills

dialogue.text: Parratt and Tarapot recount mass deportations. Sources speak of tens of thousands marched east to Ava—leaving behind fields, shrines and the bones of ancestors.

panels.shot: medium close-up of Khuman Ngamba glancing back at the receding valley through tears, the line of captives stretching ahead

dialogue.speaker: Khuman Ngamba
dialogue.text: If my body goes to Ava, let my heart stay in Kangla.

panels.shot: wide shot of the abandoned Manipur valley, with overgrown paddy and empty homesteads under grey clouds

dialogue.text: Later accounts estimate that only a few thousand remained in the valley. A land once crowded with life was left to silence, hunger and slow, creeping grass.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of a thatched hut in the hills, lit by a small fire, with exiles huddled together

dialogue.text: Many fled to Cachar, to the Naga and Kuki hills, to Assam. In strange lands they clung to words—names of rivers, gods, kings—to keep Manipur alive in memory.

panels.shot: wide shot of the Ava plain with horsemen drilling, banners fluttering, and a distant palace skyline

dialogue.text: In Ava, deported Manipuris became known as Cassay. Thant Myint-U notes them as skilled cavalrymen in Burmese service—warriors from a lost valley, now woven into another king’s army.

panels.shot: medium shot of Khuman Ngamba seated at night by a campfire outside Ava, staring at a small Kangla token

dialogue.speaker: Khuman Ngamba
dialogue.text: They can command my horse, not my dreams.

panels.shot: wide forest shot of Meitei exiles and Cachari allies listening to a messenger in a clearing

dialogue.text: Far from Ava, in the forests of Cachar, Meitei princes in exile plotted return. Rumours rode with the rains—of British moves against Burma, of new chances to reclaim Kangla.

panels.shot: dynamic mid-shot of Khuman Ngamba tightening a sword belt, with a British officer and Meitei prince in the blurred background

dialogue.text: As the First Anglo-Burmese War unfolded, exiled Manipuris aligned with British campaigns. Politics had once invited Ava; now, new politics promised a path home.

panels.shot: epic low-angle of Meitei-led forces advancing towards Manipur valley, hills opening up ahead

dialogue.speaker: Khuman Ngamba
dialogue.text: Seven years we walked in exile. Today, we walk home.

panels.shot: wide, quiet shot of re-entered Kangla—ruined, overgrown, yet familiar

dialogue.text: By 1826, Burmese forces withdrew under treaty pressures and war. The Meitei returned to a capital scarred and emptied, but still standing by the Imphal river.

panels.shot: medium shot of villagers reunited, embracing in the courtyard of a partly rebuilt homestead

dialogue.text: Families stitched themselves together from fragments—those who survived Ava, those who hid in the hills, those who never returned. The kingdom lived, but changed forever.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of an elder telling the story to children around a hearth, manuscripts beside him

dialogue.text: Chronicles recorded Chahi Taret Khuntakpa in spare lines. In homes, elders filled those lines with tears, names and vows that the valley’s silence would never be forgotten.

panels.shot: final wide shot of the Manipur valley at sunrise, fields green again but Kangla’s ruins still visible

dialogue.text: The Seven Years Devastation was wrought by kings’ ambitions and armies’ orders, but endured by farmers, soldiers and exiles. Their memory turned a wound into a warning—and a people into survivors.
